_note: Hand-authored case files for the CNEOS fireball register (object 'fb'). Baked into src/data-content.js by tools/bake_content.py, same schema and same balance rule as the 41 telescope cases: every claim carries the counter-reading beside it. F-01 and F-02 were fact-checked 2026-08-22 against the primary sources listed in each entry; the CNEOS row values are not written here at all — the console reads them live from data/fireballs.json so a catalog revision propagates. F-03, F-04, F-05 and F-06 are argued from COMPUTED FIGURES across five datasets (data/fireballs.json, data/ams-reports.json, data/gmn-monthly.json, data/volcanoes.json, data/nuforc.json, data/nuclear.json); tools/fireball_rate_check.py re-derives every number they quote and fails the refresh if any has drifted. Windows are WHOLE MONTHS on purpose — comparing a partial current month against full months in earlier years biases the current year low. Claims are attributed to the video they were made in, and a case whose claim is not Loeb's carries a claim_label so the console does not caption it as his and quotes are labelled as auto-caption transcriptions rather than presented as published text.

cases.title: IM1 — the half-metre bolide that hit at 44.8 km/s
cases.observation: At 17:05:33 UTC, US Government sensors logged a fireball over the Bismarck Sea north of Manus Island, Papua New Guinea. CNEOS lists the row at 1.2°S 147.1°E, peak brightness at 18.7 km altitude, a pre-entry speed of 44.8 km/s and a total impact energy of 0.13 kt TNT — a body roughly half a metre across. As the catalog stood at the 2026-08-22 pull it was the fifth-fastest of the 360 entries that report a speed at all. Two things about that row matter more than the numbers themselves: CNEOS publishes no uncertainties on any field, and the sensors that produced it are classified, so the measurement cannot be independently audited. The published papers arguing this case quote a box centre of 1.3°S 147.6°E; the catalog now lists 1.2°S 147.1°E, having been revised in the interim.
cases.loeb_take: Siraj & Loeb reconstructed the velocity vector as hyperbolic — gravitationally unbound from the Sun at 99.999% confidence — with an asymptotic speed of 42.1 ± 5.5 km/s and a striking 58 ± 6 km/s relative to the Local Standard of Rest, which would place its origin outside the thin disk of ordinary nearby stars. In April 2022 the US Space Command chief scientist reviewed the classified data and signed a memo stating that the velocity estimate reported to NASA was sufficiently accurate to indicate an interstellar trajectory. Loeb adds two further arguments: IM1's inferred material strength ranks first out of 273 CNEOS fireballs, and it fragmented unusually low for a chondrite at that speed. In June 2023 his Galileo Project ran a magnetic-sled expedition over the CNEOS box and recovered hundreds of sub-millimetre spherules whose beryllium-lanthanum-uranium enrichment he reports as unlike any solar-system material.
cases.loeb_quote: Its high LSR speed implies a possible origin from the deep interior of a planetary system or a star in the thick disk of the Milky Way galaxy.
cases.quote_source: WITH A. SIRAJ · ASTROPHYS. J. 939:53 (2022), ABSTRACT
cases.official_explanation: The critique attacks the one number everything rests on. Brown & Borovička (ApJ 953, 2023) compared USG fireball velocities against events with independent optical or infrasound data and found 10-15 km/s uncertainties at high speeds and radiant errors above ten degrees; their conclusion is that the simplest reading of IM1 is a substantially overestimated speed — and at a lower speed the orbit is bound and ordinary. That also dissolves the strength argument, because the ablation fits that make IM1 look ultra-strong only do so at the high assumed speed; the two 'anomalies' are one measurement, not two. Hajduková et al. (A&A 691, A8, 2024) went further: with no uncertainties published, nothing in the CNEOS data can confirm or reject an interstellar origin for any nominally hyperbolic entry. On the spherules, Gallardo (2023) matched the Be-La-U enrichment pattern to coal fly ash, a common shipping-lane contaminant, and Desch and colleagues argued a half-metre body arriving at 45 km/s would have almost entirely vaporised. In 2024 a team led by Benjamin Fernando reported that the seismic pulse used to pick the search site fitted a truck driving past the Manus Island seismometer, and placed the fireball more than 150 km from where the sled ran. Loeb answered that the expedition was guided by the 11-km CNEOS satellite box rather than the seismometer, and that Fernando's own infrasound ellipse (186 by 388 km) is large enough to contain it. The most sympathetic independent verdict is Socas-Navarro (2024), who redid the statistics and put the probability of an interstellar origin at 94.1% — significant, but short of the 3-sigma a discovery claim needs.

cases.title: IM2 — the second candidate, and the problem of a single dataset
cases.observation: At 04:16:37 UTC a considerably larger bolide was logged over the North Atlantic well west of Portugal: 40.5°N 18.0°W, peak brightness at 23.0 km, 36.5 km/s, 1.1 kt of impact energy — roughly a metre across and about an order of magnitude more massive than IM1. Nothing was recovered, no independent optical or seismic detection of it has been published, and as with every CNEOS row the catalog reports no error bars.
cases.loeb_take: Siraj & Loeb identified this row as a second unbound candidate and argued the pair is the real result. Fitting a log-normal distribution to material strengths across the catalog, IM1 and IM2 rank first and third of 273 fireballs — 3.5-sigma and 2.6-sigma outliers, with a random-draw probability around one in ten thousand. Their reading is that meter-scale interstellar objects are systematically tougher than solar-system rocks, and that the implied abundance is embarrassingly large: for two such objects to be caught by Earth's atmosphere in a few years, roughly 40% of all refractory material would have to be locked up in meter-scale interstellar bodies, which they note is hard to square with ordinary planetary-system ejection.
cases.loeb_quote: If IM2 is confirmed, this implies that interstellar meteors come from a population with material strength characteristically higher than meteors originating from within the solar system.
cases.quote_source: WITH A. SIRAJ · ASTROPHYS. J. LETT. 941 (2022), ABSTRACT
cases.official_explanation: The conditional in Loeb's own sentence is the whole objection: IM2 has never been confirmed by anything outside the catalog that produced it. The April 2022 US Space Command memo covered the 2014 event only. No expedition has looked for material, no independent detection has been published, and the velocity-uncertainty critique of Brown & Borovička applies with equal force — 36.5 km/s sits in exactly the regime where they measured 10-15 km/s errors, and shaving a few km/s makes the orbit bound. The strength ranking is derived from the same lightcurve and the same speed, so it is not independent evidence but a second reading of the first measurement. Hajduková et al. (2024) surveyed every nominally hyperbolic CNEOS entry and found none that the data can settle either way. The mainstream position is not that IM2 is impossible — it is that a single un-audited catalog, with the error bars withheld, cannot carry a claim this large on its own.

cases.title: Are fireballs increasing? Three instruments, three answers
cases.observation: Three datasets can speak to this, and no two of them measure the same thing. The American Meteor Society logs EYEWITNESS REPORTS — its unit is people, not photons, so it rises when cameras, phones and audiences do. NASA/JPL CNEOS logs US Government SENSOR DETECTIONS with an energy in kilotons, immune to how many people were watching, but with a hard floor: the smallest of its 1,069 rows is 0.048 kt and only 6 fall below 0.073 kt. The Global Meteor Network runs cameras that compute an ABSOLUTE MAGNITUDE for every meteor, with no human deciding whether to file anything — but it grew from 73 stations to 1,327 across this period, is blind in daylight, and is concentrated over Europe and North America. Every one of the three has a bias that can manufacture a trend on its own. Only the statistics that normalise those biases away are worth comparing across years.
cases.loeb_take: The claim, made most carefully by the Angry Astronaut channel in August 2026, is that 2026 delivered a genuine spike in bright fireballs — and, crucially, that it is not merely an artifact of more people looking up. As put on 2026-08-23: in the first quarter alone, events drawing 50 or more reports more than doubled the recent average and events with 100-plus reports roughly doubled, so the larger, brighter events themselves increased. That is a real, checkable proposition, and it already anticipates the obvious objection rather than ignoring it. Checked against AMS itself, the figures are ACCURATE. Q1 2026 logged 25 events in the 51-99 report band against a 2021-2025 mean of 11.8, and 16 events above 100 reports against a mean of 8.8 — 41 high-report events where the recent average is 20.6. Even as a share of all events, which corrects for the dataset simply getting bigger, high-report events ran 1.715% of the total against a 1.067% norm: 1.61 times the usual proportion, the highest in the twenty years AMS publishes.
cases.loeb_quote: The signal wasn't just more people looking up. The larger, brighter events themselves increased.
cases.quote_source: ANGRY ASTRONAUT · YOUTUBE 2026-08-23 · TRANSCRIBED FROM AUTO-CAPTIONS, NOT A PUBLISHED TEXT
cases.official_explanation: The AMS figures are right and still cannot carry the conclusion, because AMS counts reporters. A growing audience does two things at once: it surfaces more events AND it gives each event more reports, pushing events UPWARD through the bins. An event drawing 20 reports in 2022 draws 45 in 2026 and leaves the 11-25 band. So the flat middle bin is not evidence against the bias — it is the bias. The diagnostic is whether well-witnessed events outgrew the dataset as a whole, and they did not: in Q1 2026 all events ran 1.23 times the 2021-2025 mean while events with 11 or more reports ran 1.21 times it. Same population, shifted rightward. CNEOS, which cannot be moved by audience at all, shows nothing: 18 events from 1 January to 15 August against a 2016-2025 range of 18 to 31, with one event at or above 1 kilotonne. But CNEOS cannot settle it either, because essentially every event in this argument sits below its floor. The tiebreaker is the Global Meteor Network, which measures brightness directly. Normalised as bright meteors (absolute magnitude -4 or brighter) per detection — a ratio that holds however many cameras are running — Q1 2026 gives 0.286% against a 2021-2025 mean of 0.264%, a factor of 1.08 against year-to-year scatter running 0.131% to 0.440%. Across January to July, 0.275% against 0.256%. Flat, at both thresholds GMN records. The obvious confound is ruled out rather than assumed: had cameras grown more sensitive, fainter detections would swell the denominator and hide a real rise, but the median absolute magnitude holds between -0.09 and +0.05 from 2021 to 2026. THREE LIMITS CUT THE OTHER WAY AND ARE STATED HERE DELIBERATELY. GMN sees nothing in daylight, and several of 2026's most prominent events were daytime — the Lake Erie bolide at 8:57 a.m. Eastern drew 222 reports across 16 states. GMN's coverage is regional, not global. Its brightest bin is small and noisy. So this is not a refutation, and the central observation stands exactly as stated. What has moved is the burden: every measure that corrects for instrument growth is flat, and the cameras built to measure brightness did not record the change.

cases.title: The 2026 outbreak — the two events the sensors actually caught
cases.observation: Across the whole of 2025 and 2026, exactly FOUR CNEOS rows fall anywhere in the regions the 2026 fireball coverage discusses. Two of them are the marquee United States events, and both match the reported sighting to the minute. On 2026-03-17 at 12:56:42 UTC a 0.37 kt bolide was logged at 41.2 N 82.0 W — the northern Ohio shore of Lake Erie — at 45.0 km altitude and 14.9 km/s. Converted to local time that is 8:56:42 a.m. Eastern Daylight — 8:57 to the nearest minute, which is exactly the time reported for the daytime Lake Erie event that drew 222 reports across 16 states and Ontario. On 2026-08-14 at 07:48:36 UTC a 0.13 kt bolide was logged at 47.7 N 119.4 W in central Washington, 30.0 km altitude, 12.2 km/s — 12:48 a.m. Pacific Daylight, against the reported 12:48 a.m. for the event seen from northern Oregon into British Columbia with more than 250 reports. A CNEOS timestamp is published to the second and a fireball is witnessed at a specific minute, so agreement to a minute is close to a unique fingerprint. These are not date coincidences: CNEOS logs two or three events a month worldwide, and matching on date alone will happily pair a South Pacific row with a roof strike in Ohio.
cases.loeb_take: These events are presented as part of a wider 2026 pattern — an unusual density of bright, well-documented, often daytime bolides, several with sonic booms, some near volcanoes, and in the strongest form of the argument connected to material shed by 3I/ATLAS. The reading offered is not that every 2026 fireball is artificial: 'only a minority of the 2026 fireballs need be artificial. The majority, I'm sure, are ordinary meteors. The statistical excess of large events is what matters.' The Washington event is a fair example of why the pattern feels striking. NASA characterised it as roughly 16 inches across and about 170 pounds, travelling near 33,000 mph, and stated that it was NOT associated with the Perseids despite arriving two days after the shower's peak — a piece of asteroidal material on an unrelated trajectory, at a moment when the shower itself was producing no comparable daytime bolides.
cases.loeb_quote: Only a minority of the 2026 fireballs need be artificial. The majority, I'm sure, are ordinary meteors. The statistical excess of large events is what matters.
cases.quote_source: ANGRY ASTRONAUT · YOUTUBE 2026-08-23 · TRANSCRIBED FROM AUTO-CAPTIONS, NOT A PUBLISHED TEXT
cases.official_explanation: Both events are ordinary in the catalog's own terms. At 0.37 kt and 0.13 kt they are unremarkable rows — the catalog's median is 0.200 kt — and both entry speeds, 14.9 and 12.2 km/s, sit at the SLOW end for a meteoroid, which is what asteroidal material on a bound solar-system orbit looks like. Anything arriving from interstellar space enters far faster: IM1 is listed at 44.8 km/s. Neither row carries the signature the interstellar reading requires. One number in circulation is worth untangling because the confusion recurs. The Washington event was described as breaking up with the energy of roughly 10 tons of TNT, while CNEOS lists 0.13 kt — 130 tons. These are different quantities: CNEOS publishes both a RADIATED energy, 3.8 x 10^10 J for this row, and a TOTAL IMPACT energy, and the radiated figure is only the fraction emitted as light. Quoting one against the other makes events look an order of magnitude apart when they are the same event. Checking the mass claim closes the loop: 7 tons at the listed 14.9 km/s yields about 0.19 kt of kinetic energy against 0.37 kt catalogued, which is the right order for a rough public figure. The deeper point is the count itself. Only four rows in two years fall in these regions — because nearly everything in this argument is below the CNEOS floor of roughly 0.05 kt. The sensors are not staying quiet about the 2026 fireballs; with a handful of exceptions they cannot see them at all. That is a limit of the instrument, not a verdict on the sky, and it is the reason this case can put two events on the map and no more.

cases.title: Fireballs and volcanoes — testing the proximity claim
cases.observation: This is the one claim in the register that could be settled by arithmetic rather than argument, because both sides of it are already on file: 883 CNEOS events with coordinates, and 1,608 volcano positions published by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information. The test asks whether fireballs fall closer to volcanoes than chance allows, using a Monte Carlo with 1,000 trials per null model. Choosing the null is the whole test. Scattering random points over the globe would be wrong, because volcanoes sit on land and cluster in arcs, so any land or latitude bias in the detections would fake an association. Two nulls are used instead, both preserving the detections' own latitude distribution: a ROTATION null applies one random longitude offset to every event at once, keeping the event set's internal clustering perfectly intact while destroying only its alignment with volcano longitudes; a SCATTER null gives each event a fresh uniform longitude. The result is the same either way. Within 100 km of a volcano: 23 events observed against 32.8 expected by chance. Within 200 km: 78 against 82.3. Within 500 km: 260 against 250.5. Median distance to the nearest volcano: 838 km observed against 854 km by chance. Not one of those is significant, and the closest bin — the one the claim is actually about — sits BELOW chance.
cases.loeb_take: The claim is that bright fireballs keep coming down at volcanoes, too often to be coincidence, and that this is one of the strongest hints that some of them are directed rather than random. It has a long pedigree in UAP research — objects reported flying through eruption plumes, hovering over craters — and 2026 supplied vivid new examples. On 2026-05-25 a green fireball appeared to strike the flank of Mayon in the Philippines while cameras watched, with a bright object seeming to rise from the same spot afterwards; PHIVOLCS said a meteor burned up high in the atmosphere and the rising object was a satellite. Weeks later another meteor was filmed above an erupting volcano elsewhere in Asia, and lights were recorded near Popocatépetl in Mexico on 2026-07-15 and again on the 28th. As put on 2026-06-16: 'another meteor appears above an erupting volcano just a couple of weeks after the first encounter just like it, and also in Asia.'
cases.loeb_quote: Another meteor appears above an erupting volcano just a couple of weeks after the first encounter just like it, and also in Asia.
cases.quote_source: ANGRY ASTRONAUT · YOUTUBE 2026-06-16 · TRANSCRIBED FROM AUTO-CAPTIONS, NOT A PUBLISHED TEXT
cases.official_explanation: The sensor record shows no association at any distance, and the reason the visual record does is stated in the coverage itself without being noticed: 'Five Vulks cameras are rolling.' PHIVOLCS — the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology — keeps cameras trained on Mayon's sky continuously, because that is what a volcano observatory is for. Active volcanoes are among the very few places on Earth with fixed cameras pointed upward twenty-four hours a day, recording, archived, and watched by people who publish what they catch. A fireball over farmland is seen by whoever happened to look up. A fireball over a monitored volcano is filmed in high definition from several angles and posted the same day. That difference alone is enough to manufacture the entire pattern, and it is exactly the kind of selection effect CNEOS does not have: its detections come from satellite sensors that do not care whether anyone is filming. So the catalog is the right instrument for this question, and it answers no. The clustering claim fails the same way — 'three in the same place' — with the median distance between an event and its nearest neighbour at 353 km against 354 km by chance, and 55 events having another within 100 km against 46.8 expected. THE LIMIT THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY IS THE SAME ONE AS EVER, AND IT IS SERIOUS: neither the Mayon event nor the 2026-06-14 fireball has a CNEOS row at all, because both sit below the catalog's 0.048 kt floor. The nearest CNEOS row to Mayon in the entire record is 312 km away and from 2015. So this test says that the events big enough for satellites to see show no volcano preference; it cannot directly test the smaller events that the cameras actually caught. What it does establish is that the association does not exist in the one dataset immune to the camera effect — which is where a real physical association should have shown up first.

cases.title: The 2013 precedent — a real change, and the wrong month to point at
cases.observation: The National UFO Reporting Center asks every witness to pick a SHAPE from a fixed list, and 'fireball' is one of the options. That makes the archive the one dataset in this register where the word means what a person decided it meant, rather than a kilotonne figure or a camera-measured magnitude — and it is exactly the field the 2013 claim is about, so it is the right file to open. nuforc.org returns 403 to a datacenter address, as several sources this project wants do; the route that works is the planetsig/ufo-reports mirror, which geocoded and time-normalised the archive in 2014 and kept the shape column. It holds 80,332 reports from 1906-11-11 to 2014-05-08, of which 78,400 carry a shape and 1,932 do not. TWO PROPERTIES OF IT GOVERN EVERYTHING BELOW. It is scrubbed: the mirror's own unscrubbed set is documented at 88,874 records and the file this project reads holds 80,332, rows with an unresolvable location or an unparseable duration having been dropped — so counts here run below NUFORC's own. And it stops in May 2014, which means it can test the 2013 half of a 2013-versus-2026 parallel and cannot test the 2026 half at all. It is also 81% United States: 65,114 of the 80,332 rows. Every share quoted here is over shape-bearing rows, and the unlabelled ones are counted apart rather than folded in.
cases.loeb_take: The claim is a historical rhyme rather than a measurement: that 2026 is not the first time a wave of fireball reports has swamped the usual statistics, and that the last time it happened was 2013 — the year of Chelyabinsk. As put on 2026-08-23, Cheryl Costa, writing the New York Skies column for the Syracuse New Times, was reviewing the NUFORC database in November 2013 and found a dramatic nationwide spike in orange and reddish fireball sightings in the first two weeks of the month: about 238 reports logged as of the 11th, roughly average in overall volume, but about 50 of them — near 20% — of the fireball variety, against a normal share near 7% that ranked fourth among roughly 30 categories. THE BASELINE FIGURES ARE ESSENTIALLY EXACT. Across the whole archive, fireball is 6,208 of 78,400 shape-bearing reports — 7.92% — and it ranks fourth of 29 shapes, behind light (21.1%), triangle (10.0%) and circle (9.7%). Against 'about 7%, fourth of roughly 30', that is as good as a remembered statistic gets. The November elevation is real too. Through the 11th the archive holds 262 shape-bearing reports with 37 fireballs, 14.1%; restricted to the United States, which is what 'nationwide' means here, 226 reports and 33 fireballs, 14.6%. The volume figure lands almost on the nose — 227 US rows against 'about 238'. So the shape of the claim survives contact with the data: an ordinary month by volume, running roughly twice the long-run fireball share.
cases.loeb_quote: Roughly 50 of them, about 20%, were of that fireball variety. Normally these ranked fourth among roughly 30 categories and only make up about 7% of sightings.
cases.quote_source: ANGRY ASTRONAUT · YOUTUBE 2026-08-23, RELAYING CHERYL COSTA · TRANSCRIBED FROM AUTO-CAPTIONS, NOT A PUBLISHED TEXT
cases.official_explanation: What the month is measured AGAINST is where it comes apart, and the answer is more interesting than a correction. The 7.92% figure is the average of the whole archive, and the archive is more than a century long. The fireball share was not 7.92% in 2013 and had not been for years. Annually: 5.28% in 2003, 4.85% in 2004, 5.62% in 2008, 5.86% in 2009 — then 8.56%, 10.72%, 14.54%, 13.97% through 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013. The share roughly TRIPLED across four years and then stayed there. Pool the twelve months immediately before the one in question, November 2012 through October 2013, and the fireball share is 14.33%. November 2013 came in at 14.37% for the full month and 14.1% through the 11th. It was not a spike against the baseline that was current; it was that baseline, to two decimal places. Ranked against every complete month from January 2000 to April 2014 — 172 of them, none missing — it comes 14th, and the record holder is July 2012 at 22.26% (195 of 876), comfortably clear of it. FOUR THINGS CUT THE OTHER WAY AND BELONG HERE. First and largest: the tripling is real, unexplained, and precisely the kind of change the claim is reaching for — the column found the right dataset and pointed at the wrong month, three years late. NUFORC cannot say whether that rise was the sky, the arrival of a camera in every pocket, or the word 'fireball' spreading through popular usage, and this project cannot say either. Second, the shape field is a self-assigned label; 'fireball' here is what a witness called it, not a measurement, and it is not the same quantity AMS or CNEOS report under that name. Third, the archive is a scrubbed mirror of a database that is itself edited after the fact, and Costa was reading it live in November 2013 — her snapshot is not reproducible, and the gap between her roughly 50 fireballs and the mirror's 33 US ones is the size of that difference. Fourth, and it constrains the whole comparison: the mirror ends 2014-05-08, so nothing in 2026 can be checked against it. What the archive does show, twice, is that the label carries real signal. Fireball share is seasonal exactly where it should be — 10.94% in July and 10.11% in December against 6.03% in April, which is the Perseids and the Geminids appearing in a database of public shape guesses. And it shows what the archive cannot see: on 2013-02-15, the day Chelyabinsk exploded over Russia, NUFORC logged 11 reports, 2 of them fireball, and February 2013 finished at 8.08% — among the quietest months of its year. The largest airburst since Tunguska is essentially absent from it, because it happened where the reporters are not. That is the honest summary of this file: the 2013 precedent is real as a change in the record and ordinary as a month, and this dataset can neither confirm nor deny the 2026 half of the parallel it was offered for.

cases.title: Fireballs and nuclear sites — the oldest positional claim, and the wrong instrument for it
cases.observation: In early December 1948 aircrews over New Mexico began reporting brilliant green objects that flew too slowly and too flatly to be meteors. The Air Force put Dr Lincoln LaPaz, the University of New Mexico meteoriticist who had built the country's first serious fireball-recovery programme, onto the problem. His conclusion unsettled everyone: the green fireballs were not ordinary meteors, and they appeared preferentially near the installations that mattered most — Los Alamos, Sandia, Kirtland. Project Sign and then Project Grudge investigated. The public verdict settled on unusual natural phenomena; LaPaz never accepted it. THIS FILE TESTS WHAT CAN BE TESTED AND SAYS PLAINLY WHAT CANNOT. The console ships 883 CNEOS events with coordinates, and the World Resources Institute publishes positions for 195 nuclear power reactors across 31 countries. That supports the same Monte Carlo that answered the volcano claim in F-05. It does not support the claim LaPaz actually made, for two reasons that belong here rather than in a footnote. The CNEOS record begins on 1988-04-15, forty years after his fireballs, so none of his events are in it. And these are POWER REACTORS: the weapons complex he was talking about is a few dozen sites with no openly licensed positional dataset, far too few for a Monte Carlo to say anything about.
cases.loeb_take: The nuclear connection is the most persistent positional claim in the whole subject, and it is not one man's. LaPaz's green fireballs are the opening chapter; the body of it is testimony gathered over decades from people who worked at the sites — the March 1967 Malmstrom Air Force Base episode in which a flight of Minuteman missiles is reported to have gone off alert while an object hovered above, the December 1980 Rendlesham Forest sightings beside the Bentwaters weapons store, and the interviews Robert Hastings assembled from former missile officers. The shape of the claim is consistent across all of it: whatever these objects are, they take an interest in fissile material and in the machinery built around it, and they have done so since the first bombs were assembled. Stated at that level the claim is not vague and it is not trivial — it predicts a real spatial preference, and it has a large and specific evidentiary base behind it in the form of first-hand accounts from people with clearances and careers to lose.
cases.loeb_quote: He also noted that the green fireballs seemed to appear preferentially near sensitive military and scientific installations.
cases.quote_source: ANGRY ASTRONAUT · YOUTUBE · TRANSCRIBED FROM AUTO-CAPTIONS, NOT A PUBLISHED TEXT
cases.official_explanation: START WITH WHAT THIS TEST CANNOT DO, because it is most of the answer. Every event in the CNEOS catalog is an atmospheric airburst — a rock arriving at tens of kilometres per second and releasing energy in kilotonnes. The nuclear-connection testimony describes something else entirely: structured objects, often hovering, observed from the ground by guards and officers at close range. Those are not the same phenomenon, and a null result in a catalog of bolides cannot refute a body of eyewitness accounts about craft over silos. It is the wrong instrument, and the honest thing is to say so before running anything. THE SIZE FLOOR MAKES THAT WORSE, and it is the limit that matters most. The smallest row in the catalog is 0.048 kt and only 195 of 1069 fall below 0.1 kt — energies that take a metre-scale rock arriving at tens of kilometres per second. The objects in this testimony are routinely described as far smaller than that: beach-ball scale, motorcycle scale, something a guard could see the shape of. Nothing that size deposits enough energy to register here at any distance from anything, so most of the phenomenon the claim describes is excluded from the dataset before the geometry is even considered. Nor is there a better public dataset to switch to. Camera networks like the Global Meteor Network solve for meteor trajectories and discard anything that does not fit that model; satellite imagery is far too coarse; infrasound arrays have the same energy floor. The only instruments that record small, slow objects at all are human ones — sighting databases such as NUFORC, whose limits are laid out in F-06, and the official US UAP reporting, which publishes narrative case summaries rather than coordinates and so cannot feed a test of this kind either. What the catalog CAN answer is narrower and still worth having: does the population of objects large enough for satellites to detect show any positional preference for nuclear sites? Run against 195 reactors with the same two nulls used in F-05 — both preserving each event's own latitude, one rotating the whole set by a single random longitude offset and one redrawing every longitude independently, 600 trials each — the answer is mostly no, with one honest exception that is reported here rather than buried. Within 100 km: 11 events observed against 8.8 expected, p=0.290 and 0.248. Within 500 km: 68 against 71.5, p=0.702 and 0.692 — below chance. Median distance to the nearest reactor: 2682 km observed against 2687 and 2690 by chance, p=0.592 and 0.448. THE EXCEPTION IS THE MIDDLE BIN. Within 200 km there are 34 events against 24.8 expected — a 37% excess, and it reaches p=0.025 under the scatter null, though only p=0.070 under the rotation null, which is the conservative one because it leaves the events' own clustering intact. Two things keep that from being a result. Three radii were tested, and one marginal value among three correlated tests is close to what chance produces. More telling is the SHAPE: a real proximity effect is strongest where the proximity is tightest, and this one is absent at 100 km, present at 200 km, and gone again at 500 km. A bump in the middle with nothing at the centre is not what an attraction looks like. Restricting to the 85 reactors already commissioned by 1990 — the ones that existed for most of the catalog's span — leaves 22 events within 200 km and a median of 3266 km, no better. ONE MORE THING THE TARGET LIST GETS WRONG. The association as it is usually stated is with radiation and fissile material in general, not with weapons specifically — which would take in research reactors, enrichment and reprocessing plants, spent-fuel and waste storage, and industrial and medical sources. What is tested here is 195 civil POWER reactors, because that is the only category with an openly licensed global position list.
